title: Act I, Scene VII

teacherSummary.text: Alone during the feast, Macbeth weighs the murder ('If it were done when 'tis done'): Duncan is his kinsman, king and guest and a virtuous ruler, and 'bloody instructions' return to plague the inventor; he has only 'vaulting ambition.' He tells Lady Macbeth they will proceed no further. She attacks his manhood, says she would have dashed out her nursing baby's brains had she sworn to, and lays out the plan to drug the chamberlains and blame them. Macbeth agrees: 'False face must hide what the false heart doth know.'

writingPrompts.label: Middle School
writingPrompts.text: Excerpt-based (Middle School support track; this play is above the grades 6–8 complexity band, so work from the passage your teacher selects). In “Act I, Scene VII,” how does Shakespeare show the decision to murder? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the passage, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the imagery you noticed as one piece of evidence.

writingPrompts.label: HS Freshman
writingPrompts.text: In Act I, Scene VII, how does Shakespeare develop the idea of the decision to murder? State a clear claim, support it with two or three quotations, and explain how the imagery in the scene helps build that idea.

writingPrompts.label: HS Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how Act I, Scene VII develops the idea of the decision to murder. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of imagery and conflict shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.

writingPrompts.label: HS Junior
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how the structure of Act I, Scene VII (where it begins, turns and ends) and its imagery shape the reader's understanding of the decision to murder. Identify one place where the text leaves matters uncertain and explain how that uncertainty adds to its meaning.

writingPrompts.label: HS Senior
writingPrompts.text: Two readers disagree about what Act I, Scene VII suggests about the decision to murder. Lay out two plausible interpretations, weigh the evidence for each (including the scene's imagery and conflict), and argue for the stronger one in a sustained, well-organized essay.

writingPrompts.label: AP
writingPrompts.text: Write a literary argument in which you analyze how William Shakespeare uses imagery in Act I, Scene VII to complicate the reader's understanding of the decision to murder. Develop a defensible thesis, select evidence purposefully, and explain how specific choices of diction and syntax create meaning.

writingPrompts.label: College Freshman
writingPrompts.text: Situate Act I, Scene VII within its historical and literary context and argue how the scene's treatment of the decision to murder responds to that context. Engage with at least one secondary perspective (a critic, historian or the author's own statements), integrate quotations smoothly, and cite in MLA style.

writingPrompts.label: College Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Read Act I, Scene VII alongside the conventions of its genre and period. Argue how the scene's handling of the decision to murder follows or bends those conventions, using the imagery as evidence, and test your reading against one published critic. Document two secondary sources in MLA.

writingPrompts.label: College Junior
writingPrompts.text: Apply a named critical approach (for example formalist, historicist, feminist, psychoanalytic or ecocritical) to Act I, Scene VII and its treatment of the decision to murder. State your method, show what it reveals in the scene's imagery and conflict, and identify where the text resists it.

writingPrompts.label: College Senior
writingPrompts.text: Develop a research argument that reads Act I, Scene VII as evidence for a larger claim about the decision to murder in Macbeth. Connect close reading of the scene to the whole play, engage at least four scholarly sources, and state precisely where your reading departs from theirs (Chicago style).

writingPrompts.label: Graduate / PhD
writingPrompts.text: Develop an original argument that reads Act I, Scene VII as a hinge in the play's larger treatment of the decision to murder. Position your reading within a named critical conversation (for example formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist or postcolonial approaches), account for the textual history where relevant, and articulate the stakes of your intervention for scholarship on Macbeth.

segments.activity: Respond in writing to the bell-ringer, then pair-share.
segments.script: Settle in and write for five minutes: Have you ever been talked into something you had decided not to do? What arguments worked on you? No wrong answers yet; we will test these ideas against the text. Two volunteers share, and I note key words on the board. Before we start, a content note: Lady Macbeth uses a shocking image of harming a baby to make a point.

segments.activity: Introduce 5 key words: pronounce, define from context, then the word's history.
segments.script:
Today's words are chalice, daggers, ingredients, fitness, compose. For each one we read the sentence, guess from context and then check the definition. Here is the first: “But in these cases
We still have judgment here; that we but teach
Bloody instructions, which, being taught, return
To plague the inventor: this even-handed justice
Commends the ingredients of our poison’d chalice
To our own lips.” In this sentence it means: a ceremonial drinking cup. Word histories: For the other words, look up the word history (Etymonline or the OED) and record the language of origin and the root meaning in your etymology log.

segments.activity: Present the historical and literary background.
segments.script: Here is what the first readers of Macbeth would have known. The soliloquy draws on Christian ideas of judgment ('the life to come') and on the belief that a king's murder upset the whole order of nature and heaven. Why does this scene matter? This is the hinge of Act I: Macbeth's conscience reasons clearly against the deed, and Lady Macbeth defeats reason by redefining courage and manhood. The scene sets up the play's question of who is responsible. Write down one question you want answered.

segments.activity: Teacher models a think-aloud on the anchor passage for imagery.
segments.script:
Watch me read this the way a careful reader does. The passage opens: “Was the hope drunk
Wherein you dress’d yourself?” I stop and ask: what is the author doing here, and how does it connect to the decision to murder? I circle “ornament”, one of today's words, and ask why the author chose it over a plainer word. When I find imagery, I underline it and write its effect in the margin, then I check my idea against the next sentence.

segments.activity: Read the anchor passage aloud together; annotate for imagery.
segments.script: Now we do it together. I read the first sentence and you track along. Mark every example of imagery. Turn to a partner: what does the author want us to notice? I will collect three ideas and we choose the strongest using evidence.

Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of imagery and conflict shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.) I will circulate and conference.

segments.activity: Structured discussion from the 30 tiered questions (focus set for the class level): wait time, think-pair-share on DOK 3/4, follow-up probes.
segments.script: Let's talk. We move from what happens to why it matters to whether it's right. After each question I wait before calling on anyone: think first. Our anchor question: How does this scene connect to ambition and its costs? Every claim needs a page reference. Respond to the person before you by agreeing, extending or challenging with evidence, and end by writing one question of your own.

segments.activity: Scene quiz in the app, then a one-sentence exit ticket.
segments.script: Take the scene quiz in the app. Then, in one sentence, tell me what this scene suggests about the decision to murder, backed by one short quotation.

segments.activity: Summarize the lesson and preview the next reading.
segments.script: Today we saw how imagery shapes the decision to murder. Tonight, read the next scene and add two words to your etymology log.

routine: Bell-ringer: post one literal and one evaluative question; students jot before talking (wait time).
Discussion (10 min): run the focus questions for the class level in order, literal to evaluative; think-pair-share every DOK 3/4 item.
After each answer, use a follow-up probe before moving on; ask a second student to agree, extend or challenge.
Exit: each student writes one question of their own (student-generated) for tomorrow’s opener.
